Lecture 31

The wave equation and d’Alembert’s formula

We find the characteristic lines of the wave equation, write every solution as a sum of two travelling waves and derive d’Alembert’s formula for the infinite string. We prove the conservation of energy and the uniqueness it gives on a bounded string, and give a plucked string a precisely stated weaker solution.

By the end of this lecture you will be able to:

  • Derive the characteristic lines and the general solution F(x−ct)+G(x+ct)F(x-ct)+G(x+ct)F(x−ct)+G(x+ct).
  • Solve the infinite string by d’Alembert’s formula and find the initial interval on which the displacement at a given point depends.
  • Distinguish displacement data from velocity data, and compute the energy of a solution.
  • Prove uniqueness on a bounded string by energy, and state how a plucked string solves the equation.

Lecture 29 derived the equation utt=c2uxx+f/ρu_{tt}=c^2u_{xx}+f/\rhoutt​=c2uxx​+f/ρ of a stretched string with the wave speed c=T/ρc=\sqrt{T/\rho}c=T/ρ​. In this lecture we solve it without external force on the whole line. This infinite string models a long string far from its ends, before a disturbance reaches an end. The lecture reads in three stages: characteristics and d’Alembert’s formula (Sections 31.1–31.3), pulses and energy (Sections 31.4–31.5), and the plucked string and the fixed end (Sections 31.6–31.7).

31.1 Characteristics of the wave operator

Throughout the lecture c>0c>0c>0 is a constant, and the wave equation is utt=c2uxx.u_{tt}=c^2u_{xx}.utt​=c2uxx​.(31.1) It is Lecture 29’s string equation with f=0f=0f=0, and it is hyperbolic in Lecture 29’s classification. A classical solution on an open set is a function with continuous partial derivatives up to order two there that satisfies (31.1) at every point.

utt=c2uxx.u_{tt}=c^2u_{xx}.utt​=c2uxx​.(31.1)

Lecture 29’s Cauchy data on a curve, the values of uuu and of its derivative across the curve, give uxu_xux​ and utu_tut​ on the curve. As Lecture 30 announced, the characteristic curves are those on which these values and the equation fail to determine the second derivatives.

Proposition 31.1 (Second derivatives from data on a curve). Let uuu be a classical solution of (31.1) on an open set that contains the curve μ↦(x(μ),t(μ))\mu\mapsto(x(\mu),t(\mu))μ↦(x(μ),t(μ)) on an open interval, with xxx and ttt continuously differentiable and (x′,t′)≠(0,0)(x',t')\ne(0,0)(x′,t′)=(0,0). Then at each point of the curve x′uxx+t′uxt= ⁣d ⁣dμ[ux(x(μ),t(μ))],x′uxt+t′utt= ⁣d ⁣dμ[ut(x(μ),t(μ))],−c2uxx+utt=0.\begin{aligned} x'u_{xx}+t'u_{xt}&=\frac{\dd}{\dd\mu}\bigl[u_x(x(\mu),t(\mu))\bigr],\\ x'u_{xt}+t'u_{tt}&=\frac{\dd}{\dd\mu}\bigl[u_t(x(\mu),t(\mu))\bigr],\\ -c^2u_{xx}+u_{tt}&=0 . \end{aligned}x′uxx​+t′uxt​x′uxt​+t′utt​−c2uxx​+utt​​=dμd​[ux​(x(μ),t(μ))],=dμd​[ut​(x(μ),t(μ))],=0.​(31.2) The determinant of this linear system for (uxx,uxt,utt)(u_{xx},u_{xt},u_{tt})(uxx​,uxt​,utt​) is x′2−c2t′2x'^2-c^2t'^2x′2−c2t′2. At a point where x′2≠c2t′2x'^2\ne c^2t'^2x′2=c2t′2, the values of uxu_xux​ and utu_tut​ along the curve determine the second derivatives.

Proof. The first two equations are the chain rule (GM 36) applied to uxu_xux​ and utu_tut​, which are continuously differentiable, along the curve. We use utx=uxtu_{tx}=u_{xt}utx​=uxt​ (Schwarz’s theorem, GM 37). The third is the wave equation. Expanding along the first row, det⁡(x′t′00x′t′−c201)=x′(x′−0)−t′(0+c2t′)=x′2−c2t′2.\det\begin{pmatrix}x'&t'&0\\0&x'&t'\\-c^2&0&1\end{pmatrix} =x'(x'-0)-t'\bigl(0+c^2t'\bigr)=x'^2-c^2t'^2 .det​x′0−c2​t′x′0​0t′1​​=x′(x′−0)−t′(0+c2t′)=x′2−c2t′2. Where it is nonzero, the system has exactly one solution. ■

Definition 31.2 (Characteristic curve of the wave operator). A characteristic curve of the wave operator ∂t2−c2∂x2\partial_t^2-c^2\partial_x^2∂t2​−c2∂x2​ is a curve μ↦(x(μ),t(μ))\mu\mapsto(x(\mu),t(\mu))μ↦(x(μ),t(μ)) on an open interval, with xxx and ttt continuously differentiable and (x′,t′)≠(0,0)(x',t')\ne(0,0)(x′,t′)=(0,0), such that x′(μ)2=c2 t′(μ)2for every μ.x'(\mu)^2=c^2\,t'(\mu)^2\qquad\text{for every }\mu .x′(μ)2=c2t′(μ)2for every μ.(31.3)

The characteristic curves lie on straight lines. Indeed, t′(μ)=0t'(\mu)=0t′(μ)=0 would give x′(μ)=0x'(\mu)=0x′(μ)=0 by (31.3), which is excluded. So the continuous t′t't′ has one sign, ttt is strictly monotone with a differentiable inverse μ(t)\mu(t)μ(t) (GM 8), and the curve is the graph of X(t)=x(μ(t))X(t)=x(\mu(t))X(t)=x(μ(t)) with X′=x′/t′X'=x'/t'X′=x′/t′. By (31.3) the continuous function X′X'X′ takes only the values ccc and −c-c−c, so by the intermediate value theorem (GM 6) it is constant. Therefore every characteristic curve lies on a line x−ct=constorx+ct=const.x-ct=\text{const}\qquad\text{or}\qquad x+ct=\text{const}.x−ct=constorx+ct=const.(31.4) These are the two families announced by Lecture 30. A disturbance that follows the first family moves to the right with the speed ccc, and one that follows the second moves to the left.

x−ct=constorx+ct=const.x-ct=\text{const}\qquad\text{or}\qquad x+ct=\text{const}.x−ct=constorx+ct=const.(31.4)

Theorem 31.3 (General solution of the wave equation). Let uuu have continuous partial derivatives up to order two on the half-plane t>0t>0t>0. Then uuu solves (31.1) there if and only if there are functions FFF and GGG with continuous second derivatives on R\RR such that u(x,t)=F(x−ct)+G(x+ct)(x∈R, t>0).u(x,t)=F(x-ct)+G(x+ct)\qquad(x\in\R,\ t>0).u(x,t)=F(x−ct)+G(x+ct)(x∈R, t>0).(31.7) The pair (F,G)(F,G)(F,G) is unique up to replacing it by (F+b,G−b)(F+b,G-b)(F+b,G−b) with a constant bbb.

The function FFF is the right-moving profile and GGG the left-moving profile. In this lecture FFF is not a force and GGG is not a Green function. The term F(x−ct)F(x-ct)F(x−ct) is a travelling wave: at the time ttt its graph is the graph of FFF shifted to the right by ctctct.

The same proof gives (31.7) for solutions on the whole plane. The data of a problem must fix the two functions FFF and GGG.

31.3 The Cauchy problem and d’Alembert’s formula

At t=0t=0t=0 the string has an initial displacement u0u_0u0​ and an initial velocity v0v_0v0​. The wave equation is of second order in time, so it takes both, as Lecture 29 explained for Cauchy data. The line t=0t=0t=0 has the tangent (x′,t′)=(1,0)(x',t')=(1,0)(x′,t′)=(1,0), and 1≠0=c2t′21\ne0=c^2t'^21=0=c2t′2, so by Proposition 31.1 it is not characteristic.

Definition 31.4 (Classical solution of the Cauchy problem). Let u0u_0u0​ have a continuous second derivative and v0v_0v0​ a continuous first derivative on R\RR. A classical solution of the Cauchy problem utt=c2uxx(x∈R, t>0),u(x,0)=u0(x),ut(x,0)=v0(x)(x∈R),u_{tt}=c^2u_{xx}\quad(x\in\R,\ t>0),\qquad u(x,0)=u_0(x),\qquad u_t(x,0)=v_0(x)\quad(x\in\R),utt​=c2uxx​(x∈R, t>0),u(x,0)=u0​(x),ut​(x,0)=v0​(x)(x∈R),(31.8) is a function uuu that is continuous on R×[0,∞)\R\times[0,\infty)R×[0,∞), has continuous partial derivatives up to order two on R×(0,∞)\R\times(0,\infty)R×(0,∞), with utu_tut​ extending continuously to R×[0,∞)\R\times[0,\infty)R×[0,∞), that solves the wave equation for t>0t>0t>0 and satisfies the two initial conditions. Here ut(x,0)u_t(x,0)ut​(x,0) is the value of the continuous extension.

Theorem 31.5 (d’Alembert’s formula). Under the hypotheses of Definition 31.4 the Cauchy problem (31.8) has exactly one classical solution. It is u(x,t)=12[u0(x−ct)+u0(x+ct)]+12c∫x−ctx+ctv0(y) ⁣dy.u(x,t)=\frac12\bigl[u_0(x-ct)+u_0(x+ct)\bigr]+\frac1{2c}\int_{x-ct}^{x+ct}v_0(y)\dd y .u(x,t)=21​[u0​(x−ct)+u0​(x+ct)]+2c1​∫x−ctx+ct​v0​(y)dy.(31.9)

Proof. First, uniqueness. Let uuu be a classical solution. By Theorem 31.3, u=F(x−ct)+G(x+ct)u=F(x-ct)+G(x+ct)u=F(x−ct)+G(x+ct) for t>0t>0t>0, with FFF and GGG twice continuously differentiable on R\RR. Then ut=−cF′(x−ct)+cG′(x+ct)u_t=-cF'(x-ct)+cG'(x+ct)ut​=−cF′(x−ct)+cG′(x+ct) for t>0t>0t>0. Letting t→0+t\to0^+t→0+ and using the continuity of FFF, GGG, F′F'F′ and G′G'G′, of uuu and of the extension of utu_tut​, the initial conditions give F(x)+G(x)=u0(x),−F′(x)+G′(x)=v0(x)c(x∈R).F(x)+G(x)=u_0(x),\qquad -F'(x)+G'(x)=\frac{v_0(x)}c\qquad(x\in\R).F(x)+G(x)=u0​(x),−F′(x)+G′(x)=cv0​(x)​(x∈R). By the fundamental theorem of calculus (GM 26) the second equation gives G(x)−F(x)=c−1∫0xv0(y) ⁣dy+bG(x)-F(x)=c^{-1}\int_0^xv_0(y)\dd y+bG(x)−F(x)=c−1∫0x​v0​(y)dy+b with a constant bbb. Adding and subtracting the first equation, F(x)=12u0(x)−12c∫0xv0(y) ⁣dy−b2,G(x)=12u0(x)+12c∫0xv0(y) ⁣dy+b2.F(x)=\frac12u_0(x)-\frac1{2c}\int_0^xv_0(y)\dd y-\frac b2,\qquad G(x)=\frac12u_0(x)+\frac1{2c}\int_0^xv_0(y)\dd y+\frac b2 .F(x)=21​u0​(x)−2c1​∫0x​v0​(y)dy−2b​,G(x)=21​u0​(x)+2c1​∫0x​v0​(y)dy+2b​. Substituting x−ctx-ctx−ct into FFF and x+ctx+ctx+ct into GGG, the constants cancel and the two integrals combine into one integral from x−ctx-ctx−ct to x+ctx+ctx+ct. This is (31.9). So every classical solution equals the right side of (31.9).

Next, existence. Let P(x)=∫0xv0(y) ⁣dyP(x)=\int_0^xv_0(y)\dd yP(x)=∫0x​v0​(y)dy. Then P′=v0P'=v_0P′=v0​ has a continuous derivative, so PPP has a continuous second derivative. The right side of (31.9) is F(x−ct)+G(x+ct)F(x-ct)+G(x+ct)F(x−ct)+G(x+ct) with F=12u0−P/(2c)F=\tfrac12u_0-P/(2c)F=21​u0​−P/(2c) and G=12u0+P/(2c)G=\tfrac12u_0+P/(2c)G=21​u0​+P/(2c), both twice continuously differentiable on R\RR. By Theorem 31.3 it solves the wave equation. It is in fact twice continuously differentiable on the whole plane, so it is continuous on R×[0,∞)\R\times[0,\infty)R×[0,∞) and all its derivatives up to order two extend to t=0t=0t=0. At t=0t=0t=0 the integral is over a point, so u(x,0)=u0(x)u(x,0)=u_0(x)u(x,0)=u0​(x), and ut(x,0)=12[−cu0′(x)+cu0′(x)]+12c[cv0(x)+cv0(x)]=v0(x).u_t(x,0)=\frac12\bigl[-cu_0'(x)+cu_0'(x)\bigr]+\frac1{2c}\bigl[cv_0(x)+cv_0(x)\bigr]=v_0(x).ut​(x,0)=21​[−cu0′​(x)+cu0′​(x)]+2c1​[cv0​(x)+cv0​(x)]=v0​(x).■

The formula has two parts. The displacement data split into two halves, one moving to the right and one to the left, each with half the original height. The velocity data enter through their integral over an interval that grows with time.

The value of uuu at a point (x0,t0)(x_0,t_0)(x0​,t0​) with t0>0t_0>0t0​>0 uses u0u_0u0​ only at the two points x0±ct0x_0\pm ct_0x0​±ct0​ and v0v_0v0​ only on the interval [x0−ct0,x0+ct0][x_0-ct_0,x_0+ct_0][x0​−ct0​,x0​+ct0​]. This interval is the domain of dependence of the point. It is cut out of the initial line by the two characteristic lines through (x0,t0)(x_0,t_0)(x0​,t0​), which bound a triangle in the (x,t)(x,t)(x,t)-plane (Figure 31.1). Conversely, the data near a point x1x_1x1​ affect u(x,t)u(x,t)u(x,t) only if x1x_1x1​ lies in [x−ct,x+ct][x-ct,x+ct][x−ct,x+ct], that is, only in the wedge ∣x−x1∣≤ct\abs{x-x_1}\le ct∣x−x1​∣≤ct above x1x_1x1​. This wedge is the domain of influence of x1x_1x1​. In particular, if u0u_0u0​ and v0v_0v0​ vanish outside an interval [x1,x2][x_1,x_2][x1​,x2​], then u(x,t)=0wheneverx<x1−ctorx>x2+ct.u(x,t)=0\qquad\text{whenever}\qquad x<x_1-ct\quad\text{or}\quad x>x_2+ct .u(x,t)=0wheneverx<x1​−ctorx>x2​+ct.(31.10) Disturbances travel with at most the speed ccc. This property is called finite propagation speed.

u(x,t)=0wheneverx<x1−ctorx>x2+ct.u(x,t)=0\qquad\text{whenever}\qquad x<x_1-ct\quad\text{or}\quad x>x_2+ct .u(x,t)=0wheneverx<x1​−ctorx>x2​+ct.(31.10)

Formula (31.9) also shows that the solution changes little when the data change little. This is the continuous dependence required of a well-posed problem in Lecture 29.

Proposition 31.6 (Continuous dependence on the data). 31.4 Displacement and velocity pulses

31.6 A plucked string and its weaker solution

A guitar string is plucked by pulling it aside at one point and releasing it. Its initial shape has a corner, so it does not have a second derivative there, and Theorem 31.5 does not apply. The formula of d’Alembert still makes sense, and we now state in which sense it solves the problem.

Example 31.11 (A triangular pluck). We follow a string released at rest from a triangular shape and locate the points where the formula fails to be a classical solution. 31.7 A fixed end

Summary

The wave operator has the characteristic lines x±ct=constx\pm ct=\text{const}x±ct=const. In the coordinates α=x−ct\alpha=x-ctα=x−ct and β=x+ct\beta=x+ctβ=x+ct the wave equation becomes Wαβ=0W_{\alpha\beta}=0Wαβ​=0, so every classical solution is a sum of a right-moving and a left-moving wave. The initial displacement and velocity fix these waves and give d’Alembert’s formula, which depends continuously on the data and propagates disturbances with at most the speed ccc. The energy changes only by the power delivered at the ends, which proves uniqueness on a bounded string. A plucked string is described by the d’Alembert solution, a solution in the sense of distributions and a uniform limit of classical solutions.

  • General solution: for uuu with continuous second derivatives on t>0t>0t>0, utt=c2uxxu_{tt}=c^2u_{xx}utt​=c2uxx​ if and only if u=F(x−ct)+G(x+ct)u=F(x-ct)+G(x+ct)u=F(x−ct)+G(x+ct) with FFF and GGG twice continuously differentiable.

  • d’Alembert’s formula: for u0∈C2u_0\in C^2u0​∈C2 and v0∈C1v_0\in C^1v0​∈C1, u=12[u0(x−ct)+u0(x+ct)]+12c∫x−ctx+ctv0 ⁣dyu=\tfrac12[u_0(x-ct)+u_0(x+ct)]+\tfrac1{2c}\int_{x-ct}^{x+ct}v_0\dd yu=21​[u0​(x−ct)+u0​(x+ct)]+2c1​∫x−ctx+ct​v0​dy is the unique classical solution; ∣u−u~∣≤sup⁡∣u0−u~0∣+tsup⁡∣v0−v~0∣\abs{u-\tilde u}\le\sup\abs{u_0-\tilde u_0}+t\sup\abs{v_0-\tilde v_0}∣u−u~∣≤sup∣u0​−u~0​∣+tsup∣v0​−v~0​∣.

  • Domains: u(x0,t0)u(x_0,t_0)u(x0​,t0​) depends on the data in [x0−ct0,x0+ct0][x_0-ct_0,x_0+ct_0][x0​−ct0​,x0​+ct0​]; the data at x1x_1x1​ influence only ∣x−x1∣≤ct\abs{x-x_1}\le ct∣x−x1​∣≤ct.

  • Energy: E(t2)−E(t1)=∫t1t2[Tuxut]x1x2 ⁣dtE(t_2)-E(t_1)=\int_{t_1}^{t_2}[Tu_xu_t]_{x_1}^{x_2}\dd tE(t2​)−E(t1​)=∫t1​t2​​[Tux​ut​]x1​x2​​dt for e=12ρut2+12Tux2e=\tfrac12\rho u_t^2+\tfrac12Tu_x^2e=21​ρut2​+21​Tux2​. Fixed and free ends do no work, which gives uniqueness on a bounded string.
